rows: Rotavirus is an important cause of gastroenteritis in young children.
Vaccination is offered through the routine infant programme.
Laboratory surveillance tracks circulating rotavirus activity.
Hand hygiene and environmental cleaning help reduce spread.
Symptomatic children require attention to hydration.
Healthcare and childcare outbreaks require infection-control measures.
Vaccine effectiveness and safety are monitored nationally.
Vomiting, diarrhoea or vaccination status does not establish rotavirus infection.
Conclusions require symptoms, age, specimen, timing, setting, vaccination and outbreak evidence.
RSV is a common respiratory virus that can cause severe illness in infants and older or vulnerable adults.
Seasonal surveillance monitors RSV activity in England.
Clinical assessment should consider age, breathing difficulty and vulnerability.
Laboratory testing supports diagnosis in relevant settings.
Infection prevention measures are important in healthcare and care settings.
Immunisation programmes protect defined eligible groups.
Outbreaks require setting-specific control and communication.
Current surveillance and immunisation guidance should inform decisions.
A cough, bronchiolitis diagnosis or positive test does not establish the source or severity of an outbreak.
Conclusions require age, symptoms, testing, timing, setting, vulnerability, immunisation and epidemiological evidence.
Hepatitis E is a viral infection that can cause acute liver disease.
Exposure can be associated with contaminated food, water or travel.
Some infections acquired in the UK are linked to zoonotic transmission.
Diagnosis requires appropriate serological or molecular testing.
People with underlying liver disease or immune suppression may have greater risk.
Food hygiene and thorough cooking reduce relevant foodborne risk.
Persistent infection requires specialist clinical management.
Abnormal liver tests or pork consumption does not establish hepatitis E.
Conclusions require symptoms, liver tests, serology or RNA, timing, food or travel exposure and clinical evidence.
Giardiasis is an intestinal infection caused by Giardia parasites.
Transmission can occur through contaminated water, food or person-to-person spread.
Symptoms can include diarrhoea, abdominal discomfort and weight loss.
Laboratory testing of stool supports diagnosis.
Water and travel histories are relevant to investigation.
Clusters require assessment of common exposures and settings.
Diarrhoea, travel or untreated-water exposure does not establish giardiasis.
Conclusions require symptoms, stool testing, timing, water, travel, contacts, treatment and epidemiological evidence.
